title: ‘Coyote Vs. Acme’ Director Celebrates Film Release, Saying “We Won” & “It’s Proof That Movies Don’t Just Go Away”
full_text: Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando Dan Stevens Hopes Prime Video’s ‘RoboCop’ Series “Preserves” Elements Of “Extreme Violence & Also Satire” ‘Vanderpump Villa’ Renewed For Season 4 At Hulu CBS Shuts Down ‘Big Brother’ Live Feeds To Avoid Spoilers In “Unprecedented Twist”: “Go Outside, Smell The Flowers” View All August 28, 2026 1:23pm 'Coyote vs. Acme' Warner Bros. Coyote vs. Acme has made its way to theaters, and director Dave Green is expressing his gratitude. “COYOTE VS. ACME IS FINALLY, GLORIOUSLY, IN THEATERS NOW. Which means one thing. WE WON,” Green shared on Instagram. “You can go see this movie. In a theater. In your favorite seat. With your favorite snacks. With your favorite people. You can head into a dark room and laugh with strangers. Together. Congratulations to everyone who made this happen.” Green noted that the “victory” was a “shared experience,” adding, “It’s a record of the cast and crew, post, prep, and animation teams who poured so much love and passion into it over years and years.” Related Stories News 'Coyote Vs. Acme' $1.7M Previews, 'Dog Stars' $850K As Canines Rule Thursday - Box Office News 'Coyote Vs. Acme' & 'Dog Stars' Barking Up 'Spider-Man's Tree With Summer End Near - Weekend Preview “It’s shared, permanently, with the audience who fought so hard for its survival. Your fight is the reason this film finally made it to the big screen. Thank you @ketchupentertainment for hearing the audience. We’re so grateful that you did,” he continued. Watch on Deadline Coyote vs. Acme was originally set to premiere July 21, 2023, but Warner Bros. moved it to make way for Barbie . However, in November of that same year, the studio shelved the movie and instead took a $30 million tax write-off . In March 2025, Warner Bros. completed the sale of the Looney Tunes hybrid to Ketchup Entertainment, with Forte recently revealing that they plan to release the film on August 28, 2026. Green championed the effort to keep Coyote vs. Acme from remaining shelved, finding a way for audiences to finally see the movie in theaters. “This is a celebration, it’s proof that movies don’t just go away. We make work so it can be seen and shared — that’s the whole reason we do what we do,” Green said. “Persistence and resilience have truly won the day. Enjoy Coyote vs. Acm e on the big screen. Where it was always meant to be seen!” Coyote vs. Acme was written by Samy Burch, based on a story by James Gunn, Jeremy Slater, and Burch. The film follows Wile E. Coyote as he hires a billboard attorney to sue the Acme Corporation for selling faulty products. Will Forte, Lana Condor, John Cena, Luis Guzmán, and Kenneth Choi are among the actors in the cast. title: Dave Franco Says Raunchy ‘Idiots’ Scene Is “Craziest Thing” He’s Done on Camera
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All August 28, 2026 1:19pm Dave Franco attends the premiere of "Idiots" presented by IFC at Vidiots on August 10, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Logo text If you’re an emerging director, chances are you’ll hear a word of encouragement from Dave Franco . Jeremy Saulnier certainly did after the actor saw the filmmaker’s breakout self- and crowd-funded revenge thriller, Blue Ruin (2013), starring his childhood best friend Macon Blair . When Blair himself took a crack at the director’s chair a few years later, Franco also reached out to compliment his Sundance-winning I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore . The Palo Alto native admits his generosity is partly motivated by a desire to get on talented directors’ radars for future roles, but it’s mainly about softening the industry’s competitiveness. Related Stories Movies 'Idiots' Filmmaker Macon Blair Talks Surviving 13 Years of Setbacks, Recastings and a Title Change Movies What Happened to '23 Jump Street'? “We don’t tell each other enough how much we enjoy each other’s work. There’s such a competitive spirit within the industry that I just want to put out some good vibes, especially if it’s someone’s first time putting out a movie,” Franco tells The Hollywood Reporter in support of Idiots ’ Aug. 28 theatrical release. “So I guess I play the long game sometimes, but it doesn’t normally lead to collaboration. More often than not, it has led to friendship.” In Blair’s case, Franco’s overture in 2017 led to both friendship and eventual collaboration. The writer-director quickly returned the favor by sending Franco his road comedy script called The Shitheads . Franco soon realized, however, that he was too young to play the then-40-something Mark Southard, an aging slacker who, along with another underachiever named Davis Hench, winds up transporting a reprehensible trust-fund teen named Sheridan to rehab. The film would nearly go in 2017 and 2018 with a couple different combinations of actors, particularly Luke Wilson and Tracy Morgan, but then its financing came crashing down, shelving the picture until Franco wrote another one of his patented emails around 2024. At this point, he’d not only aged into the role of Mark, but he’d also directed and/or produced a number of projects to where he could be equally beneficial behind the camera. “I said, ‘No pressure, but I’m here. If I can help in any way as a producer, I’d love to come in and help find the money,’” Franco recalls. “So I’ve basically been stalking Macon for the past ten years in trying to collaborate with him.” The Shitheads did indeed find funding in 2025 en route to a fall shoot in Georgia. Franco even proved instrumental on the casting side of things by recommending O’Shea Jackson Jr. as Davis. The two actors had previously worked together on a series for the short-lived short-form platform, Quibi. And when it came time to find the despicable teenage influencer named Sheridan, Franco suggested Mason Thames from their 2025 film Regretting You . Before being retitled to Idiots , the film’s original title of The Shitheads wasn’t just a reference to Mark and Davis’ gross incompetence at life. It also had to do with the film’s signature scene in which Sheridan spikes his handlers’ generic colas, causing Mark to produce a geyser of diarrhea in their motel room. “It’s a top-three poo scene in cinematic history. It’s up there with Jeff Daniels in Dumb and Dumber ,” Franco states. “I remember calling my wife [Alison Brie] after that day and telling her I just did the craziest thing I’ve ever done on camera, which is saying a lot because I’ve done so many fucked-up things on camera. But I hold to that statement, and I’m pretty confident that it’s a violent moment people will talk about afterward.” The pic premiered at 2026’s Sundance Film Festival before securing theatrical distribution from IFC the following month. The deal was not contingent on a title change, but Team Shitheads , once they learned about the realities of promotion, realized that they’d only be making it harder for their small throwback comedy to gain traction. Thus, they landed on Idiots to keep the tontal spirit of the original intact. All in all, Franco hopes Idiots can do its part to bring back a brand of comedy that has largely disappeared from multiplexes. “ Idiots hearkens back to comedies from the early 2000s: The Hangover , Superbad , Pineapple Express , Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle ,” Franco says. “There are other moments besides the diarrhea scene that’ll shock audiences. I have personally missed these types of comedies. So I hope people check it out because, for us to be able to make more comedies again, people need to see the rare ones that do get made.” Below, during a recent conversation with THR , Franco also discusses his future as a director, before updating his status on 24 Jump Street and Now You See Me 4 . *** You don’t look like Alison Brie. ( Franco is using his wife’s Zoom account. ) I like to get people’s hopes up and then slash them when I finally appear on screen. You look more like the French Dip-hating Dave Franco . ( Laughs .) Wow, you’ve done your research. Dave Franco as Mark in Macon Blair’s Idiots Courtesy of IFC I keep tabs on the situation. So a script called The Shitheads shows up in your inbox one day. It’s from Macon Blair of Blue Ruin fame. Were you already familiar with the work he and Jeremy Saulnier have done together? Big time. I re-watch Blue Ruin every single year. It’s probably the movie I recommend to people more than any other. It was made for less than half a million dollars, and it’s a perfect, taut thriller. So that was my introduction to Macon as an actor. Then I saw the first movie he wrote and directed, I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore , and that’s when I reached out to Macon to say, “I love your shit. I will do anything with you.” This was nearly 10 years ago now [in 2017], and at the time, he sent me the script for The Shitheads . But I was too young to play the Mark role that I ultimately played. So it wasn’t meant to be, and we amicably parted ways Eight years then passed, and I reached out to him again to say, “Hey man, I’m old now. Let’s go! Whatever happened to that project?” Then he told me that it almost went, but it fell apart. So I said, “No pressure, but I’m here. If I can help in any way as a producer, I’d love to come in and help find the money.” And he said, “Alright, let’s give it a shot.” So I’ve basically been stalking Macon for the past ten years in trying to collaborate with him. Do you often play the long game? If I see a movie that I love, especially by a first-time director, I will reach out to them and let them know how much I love their work. Part of that is obviously wanting to work with them myself, but another part is that we don’t tell each other enough how much we enjoy each other’s work. There’s such a competitive spirit within the industry that I just want to put out some good vibes, especially if it’s someone’s first time putting out a movie. I just want to send them some love. So I guess I play the long game sometimes, but it doesn’t normally lead to collaboration. More often than not, it has led to friendship. I’ll meet up with people every once in a while to talk film, and one of those people is Jeremy Saulnier. I reached out to him about Blue Ruin . As you mentioned, the Shitheads script has had quite a history the last 13 years. It once had Luke Wilson and Tracy Morgan attached to it in 2017. Macon did tell me that he aged the piece down a little bit because you and O’Shea Jackson Jr. are still younger than that combo would’ve been at the time. But how noticeable were those changes from your perspective? If I’m being honest, not a ton changed. It was more just practicalities like, “Hey, we don’t have enough time or money to do some set piece, so we had to cut it.” But for the most part, the script has remained untouched, which speaks to just how timeless this story is and how iconic these characters are. It stood the test of time, and there weren’t a bunch of rewrites just to make it more modern. You’ve always been able to play younger, and I still think you can play younger. Has that been a blessing for the most part? Or has it worked against you like it originally did with The Shitheads in 2017? It’s a tough question to answer. I’m sure it’s gone both ways where it’s benefited me in certain circumstances and then been detrimental in others. But for this film, I did want to look slightly older than I typically do. I did my absolute best to grow out my facial hair, and it came in nice and scraggly. I learned that I can grow a pretty strong goatee, but the sides are nasty and patchy. So it worked beautifully for this character who’s a full-on shithead. Dave Franco as Mark in Macon Blair’s Idiots Courtesy of IFC 6 Balloons (2018) was the more dramatic portrayal, but coming out of The Studio season one’s penultimate drug episode, were you hesitant at all to play another character who’s drugged out of his mind? You’re the first person to ever connect 6 Balloons to The Studio , and I appreciate that. I played a heroin addict in 6 Balloons , and it’s a hardcore drama. Leading up to filming, I lost 20 pounds in a month. I’m not a very big guy as is, so that was a significant portion of my body weight. I was not a happy person, as you can imagine. But I wanted to take myself out of my comfort zone in order to try something new. And even though it’s a very small movie that not a ton of people have seen, it’s interesting how much it still comes up. It usually happens when directors are reaching out to me about slightly more serious projects that they’re working on, and then they’ll point to my performance in that. So it means a lot just because we put a lot into that one. But when I’m playing “Dave Franco” on The Studio — and I’m inebriated on alcohol, weed, cocaine and mushrooms at the same time — I can push the boundaries a little bit more. I can be a little sillier and a little more over the top. It’s a more manic version of being drugged out. In Idiots , my character partakes in drugs as well, but it’s a different kind of drug trip. This is more of a sink-into-the-couch type of trip. If someone says the wrong trigger word, it sends Mark spiraling into hell. So I like to believe that I have a lot of range when it comes to playing drug addicts. The funniest part of Idiots to me is how Mark is constantly trying to relate to people that he has absolutely nothing in common with, such as the scene in the bathroom with Sheridan (Mason Thames) or the scene coming out of the bathroom with the motel clerk: “You’re a man who takes pride in what he does; I am too.” Like you said, he truly is full of shit. Yeah, he really likes to believe he’s a hero, and he has a strong lack of self-awareness. He means well, but he just doesn’t know how he’s coming across to others. He says to Sheridan, “Guys like you and me, we’re used to being up in the high steel.” So there’s nothing more fun to play than a cocky fucking idiot — someone so convinced he’s a great person, and the smartest guy in the room, when in reality, he’s just a shithead. Macon explained the title saga to me, but did you fully expect the Shitheads title to change at some point? If I’m being totally honest, once we got through Sundance with that title, I had hopes that we could somehow take it to the finish line. But we had a very open, honest conversation with our distributor, IFC. And to their credit, they said, “Hey, we’re willing to ride this title. If you guys want to go punk rock, we are right there with you. But we have to let you know that it limits us in terms of where we can market this film. You can’t just have the word shit on a giant billboard in Hollywood.” Ultimately, we put so much work into this film, and because we want as many people to see it as possible, that’s why we pivoted. There’s a Lars von Trier movie called The Idiots , but no one had taken the cleaner version of Idiots , so we jumped on it. Yeah, it’s now the movie’s second Lars von Trier reference. You gotta love the double Lars von Trier reference. O’Shea Jackson Jr.’s Davis, Dave Franco’s Mark and Mason Thames’ Sheridan in Macon Blair’s Idiots Courtesy of IFC Entertainment I’m glad they kept Sheridan’s “shitheads” line in the movie as a nod to the former title and the explosive motel scene. I know they changed the line to “idiots” in the trailer, but if you were forced to do so in the movie, would you have protested that choice to ADR the new title? Yeah, there’s no reason to change that line just because that’s how it’s represented in the trailer. Just let it play out the way we intended when we shot it. O’Shea’s character goes off on Mason’s character after that “shitheads” line, and Mark quietly laughs as this mostly measured guy finally loses his cool. But I did wonder if you actually broke ever so slightly there given how sudden and strong the outburst is. That was definitely intentional. That was my character being so giddy and pleased by the fact that Sheridan is finally being put in his place. He’s also entertained by the idea of this man of God stepping outside of his comfort zone and swearing in a way that he probably never has before. So there’s a lot for Mark to be titillated by in that moment. I have to tell you a story about the time I saw Together . I was standing behind a critic as he was giving his comment to the studio rep. And he remarked, “I liked the movie, but the two leads had absolutely no chemistry.” And then the rep and I both responded in unison: “Dude, they’re married.” Hilarity then ensued once he realized his oversight, and I still tease him about it to this day. I appreciate you standing up for me, but to be fair, there are married couples that don’t have chemistry together on screen. We actually feared that that might be the case. And while I’m never one to pat myself on the back, that is not an issue with that film. The chemistry is fucking there. ( Laughs .) I think some people mistake chemistry for characters just not liking each other. So our characters are definitely at odds for most of that film, but we’re flowing off each other in an objectively smooth and electric way. Dave Franco and Alison Brie in Together Germain McMicking/Courtesy of NEON You’ve probably been told that you’ve got good chemistry with other actors throughout your career. But I always hesitate to make that assumption because only the scene partners truly know whether they have good chemistry or not. What percentage of the time is it actually good chemistry versus good acting and good editing? There’s been situations where it’s known that certain people hated each other on set, and then they have “great chemistry” when you see the final product. So there are cases like that, but more often than not, if they have good chemistry on set, you’re going to feel it when you see them on the big screen. For me, I’ve made a conscious effort, especially in the last decade, to surround myself with people that I know and love, whether that’s my best friends or my wife. When I’m surrounded by people that I feel comfortable with, that allows me to be free and open and take risks. I know I’m going to fall on my face sometimes, but I also know that no one is going to judge me. They’ll keep encouraging me to try weird shit, and that’s when the best stuff comes. I last spoke to you for The Rental , so what’s up with writer-director Dave Franco? Have Obsession and Backrooms motivated you to make another horror movie? I definitely will direct again, and I really believe that the next movie I direct will be a horror film. That said, when you’re directing something, you’re focused on that project for years at a time, and it takes everything out of you. So I’m just not currently in the state of mind to dedicate myself to one project like that. But I’ve been able to scratch that itch by being a producer on films like Idiots that I’m also acting in. I can still be a part of all the conversations from the ground up and through the release of the film. So that’s been really fun and satisfying for me, and it still allows me to bounce around to many different projects. Do you know yet if you’re going to be in 24 Jump Street ? The truth is I don’t know yet. I have let them know how much I adore the franchise and that I’m here if they need me — but if Eric Molson doesn’t naturally fit into the story, I understand. Do you think Now You 4 Me is going to happen? I think it’s going under the name of 4 Now You See Me: 4 Now You Don’t. ( Laughs .) You’ve clearly workshopped this title. ( Laughs .) I’ve heard that there’s a script in the works, but I haven’t seen anything. That’s as much as I know at this point. For the sake of inspiration, The Studio welcomed any and all industry stories from the cast and crew. Did you ever offer up your experience on the 2019 motion picture 6 Underground ? ( Laughs and responds sarcastically. ) Why do you assume that movie spawned production stories? Well, I asked you about it during The Rental , and while you said it was 50 times crazier than I could possibly imagine, you also said it was better suited for an off-the-record dinner conversation. ( Laughs .) With The Studio , the truth is I wasn’t on that set long enough for them to be mining stories from me. I wasn’t around during pre-production or the whole writing process. But 6 Underground was a whirlwind. I played a [getaway] driver who drives around the streets of Florence, Italy, but I didn’t expect to actually do a lot of the driving with Ryan Reynolds in the passenger seat — plus Mélanie Laurent and Adria Arjona in the backseat. There was a moment when I was doing donuts next to a world-famous museum in Florence, and if I hit something, I could have literally destroyed a piece of history. Looking back, it was a slightly idiotic thing to do, and I blame myself. I should have just handed the wheel over to my stunt double. Decades from now, when you and your wife are swapping set stories like the one you just shared, what day on Idiots will you likely bring up first? You know it has to be the day of the diarrhea scene. It’s a top-three poo scene in cinematic history. It’s up there with Jeff Daniels in Dumb and Dumber . I remember calling my wife after that day and telling her I just did the craziest thing I’ve ever done on camera, which is saying a lot because I’ve done so many fucked-up things on camera. But I hold to that statement, and I’m pretty confident that it’s a violent moment people will talk about afterward. The cast and crew experienced it for the first time together. We never tested the rig before cameras rolled on the day, and it was so volcanic that everyone on set immediately started cracking up. But the camera was still on me as I was losing my faculties in this delirious state, so I had to stay in character and pretend like nothing was happening. We did two takes, and on the second take, we decided to add a little texture with some mashed-up Cocoa Krispies. Raunchy comedies like this used to be common. Yeah, Idiots is meant to be a throwback comedy. It hearkens back to comedies from the early 2000s: The Hangover , Superbad , Pineapple Express , Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle . It’s a movie that goes hard. There are other moments besides the diarrhea scene that’ll shock audiences. They won’t believe how far we push things in this. I have personally missed these types of comedies, and I have heard from many other people who feel the same way. So I hope people check it out because, for us to be able to make more comedies again, people need to see the rare ones that do get made. Did the MPA force Macon to cut the diarrhea scene down at all? There was no conversation about that. They were like, “Get rid of the title Shitheads , but show the gnarliest shit scene possible.” Respect. *** Idiots is now playing in movie theaters nationwide. THR

title: ‘The Big Break’ Reboot’s Debut Season Shelved By The Golf Channel After Good Good Withdraws Title Sponsorship
full_text: Skip to main content By Denise Petski Denise Petski Senior Managing Editor More Stories By Denise Disney+ Greenlights New Pokémon Stop-Motion Series As Part Of Global Distribution Deal ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Adds J. Smith-Cameron As Recurring For Season 28 Anonymous Content Names Steve Shikiya Chief Operating Officer View All August 28, 2026 1:10pm Scottie Scheffler on the 18th hole during the first round of the Tour Championship 2026 at East Lake Golf Club, August 27, 2026, in Atlanta, GA Getty Images A major scandal that has rocked the golf world has impacted the debut season of The Golf Channel ‘s reboot of The Big Break reality competition series. The new season, which was due to premiere Tuesday, August 25, has been canceled after Good Good announced it would be stepping away as title sponsor of the Good Good Championship, a new PGA Tour event set for November in Austin, Texas. The winner of the reboot’s debut season was supposed to receive a sponsor exemption to compete in the Austin event. Since Good Good pulled out, there was no prize to be given, hence the season cancellation. Related Stories News Kai Trump To Join Golf Channel Broadcast Crew Next Weekend News The Golf Channel Picks Up Chad Mumm & Wells Adams' 'Vanity Index' As It Takes A Swing At Video Podcasts The controversy erupted a week ago when Good Good posted on its social channels a 60-second ad, which has since been taken down, depicting one of Good Good’s members knocking down a female member reaching for his golf bag and then standing over her, saying, “Do not touch my new driver.” Watch on Deadline Shortly thereafter, Callaway Golf Company, a leading American sports equipment manufacturer based in Carlsbad, CA, cut ties with Good Good amidst the outcry over the ad. Good Good then announced it was withdrawing its sponsorship for the Austin event. Golf Channel had initially postponed the series premiere, originally scheduled for this past Tuesday night, to Sept. 1. The Versant cable network then followed with a statement Thursday on social media: “Following recent developments involving Good Good, and including the fact that the intended outcome of the series can no longer be fulfilled, Golf Channel will not be able to complete this season of Big Break as planned,” Golf Channel said in the statement. “While we are disappointed for the 12 competitors, our production team that worked tirelessly on the season, and the show’s passionate fans, we look forward to Big Break’s return to Golf Channel in 2027.” The Big Break aired from 2003-2015, when the series was canceled amid cuts by Golf Channel’s then-owner NBCUniversal. In October 2025, Golf Channel announced that The Big Break would be revived for a 24th season, in collaboration with the golf-oriented media company Good Good. title: Top Toronto Fest Party Host Expects More Studio Bashes, Tighter Budgets: “No One Is Throwing Money Around”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All August 28, 2026 12:27pm TIFF Lightbox headquarters Zou Zheng/Xinhua via Getty Images Restaurant and nightclub kingpin Charles Khabouth, a top party host for major studio and streamer movie premieres at the Toronto Film Festival each year, expects to feed and honor more Hollywood A-stars in town this year for the 2026 edition. “Last year we did 46 events. This year we’re at 51 (parties) and counting,” Khabouth told The Hollywood Reporter on Friday, ahead of TIFF getting underway on Sept. 10 for an 11-day run. That’s good news for the wait and bar staff at his downtown Toronto venues around TIFF Lightbox like Vinny, Bisha Hotel, STORYS Building, Portland Room, Animl Steakhouse & Cocktail Den, Kost, Byblos and Bar Romy as prime locations for Hollywood star-watchers during the festival’s 51 st edition. Related Stories Movies Late F1 Icon Gilles Villeneuve Drives For Speed, Trophies in 'Rise of a Legend' Trailer (Exclusive) Guest Column Keep Your Opinions Off Celebrities' Bodies (Unless It's Time to Intervene) And Khabouth expects even more American players to call about late-party bookings, or to upgrade cocktail events or intimate dinners to full-blown movie premiere parties. “With last-minute changes, I estimate we will hit 60 events this year,” he added, with around 35 of those expected to be parties with an average of 200 attendees. That’s also good news for local food and alcohol suppliers, limo drivers, security personnel, tablecloth and glassware suppliers. And Toronto launching its inaugural TIFF: The Market is also predicted to offer even more business for local party suppliers, including those installing drapery, lighting and red carpets. Khabouth cautions, however, party spending by Hollywood studios and streamers this year will continue to come down in Toronto, as it has since COVID. “There’s nobody throwing money around like they used to,” the top restaurateur, who has been in business in Toronto with his Ink Entertainment banner since 1983, reported as the Hollywood bean counters are now in charge. That’s made lavish Hollywood premiere parties in Toronto, where the champagne flowed to help toast or tout upcoming award season contenders, a thing of the past. “It’s all budgeted. It’s all calculated. The studios are no longer doing what they used to. Budgets have been cut back everywhere and we understand,” Khabouth argued. That means his restaurant and nightclub venues will continue to work within the budgets of the major American players, while still offering a superior product to ensure repeat business. “It’s still important to deliver that great experience. It showcases that we’re doing a good job,” Khabouth insisted. The Toronto Film Festival is set to run Sept. 10 to 20 this year. THR

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Still in More Theaters Than Any Other Movie 5 Weekends Later
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All August 28, 2026 11:43am Tom Holland in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Logo text Stop us if you’ve heard this before: That Spider-Man: Brand New Day movie? It’s doing pretty darn well. Insanely well. Like $2.24 billion and counting worth of well. Now, going into its fifth weekend, the Sony-Marvel blockbuster is quietly showing another type of strength: Even with two new major films opening, exhibitors are keeping Brand New Day in more theaters than any other movie. It’s close, mind you, but still: Brand New Day will be in 3,678 theaters, more than any other title, just barely dropping from last weekend’s 4,006. The Looney Tunes legal comedy, Coyote vs. Acme is opening in slightly fewer theaters — 3,575 — despite very strong reviews (95 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes; read The Hollywood Reporter ‘s review ) and strong audience scores (92 percent). Coyote vs. Acme is tracking for a somewhat modest $14 million to $22 million domestic opening. While it might not prove to be a hit, its overall reception is certainly making the case that it was a movie worth releasing rather than shelving for a tax write-down, as Warner Bros. originally planned. Then there’s Ridley Scott’s post-apocalyptic thriller The Dog Stars opening right behind Coyote in 3,330 theaters (the film has largely negative reviews from critics — though THR ‘s review was positive — with a domestic opening predicted around $9 million to $14 million). But back to Brand New Day , which has been the gift that keeps on giving for Sony-Marvel and theater owners since its July 31 release. The records have piled up: Biggest opening day ($169 million), biggest domestic opening weekend ($360 million), biggest Monday ever ($47 million), the fastest movie to hit $500 million (seven days), the second-biggest movie ever domestically and, currently, the highest grossing movie of 2026. Brand New Day is expected to rack up yet another $22 million to $27 million domestically this weekend, which should put it past Titanic on the list of the highest-grossing movies of all time. THR

title: ‘The Dog Stars’: 6 Of The Biggest Changes Between Peter Heller’s Book And The Ridley Scott Film
full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi All The Songs In ‘The Dog Stars’: From Hozier To Caamp ‘The Dog Stars’: 6 Of The Biggest Changes Between Peter Heller’s Book And The Ridley Scott Film ‘In A Holidaze’ Film Adaptation Of Christina Lauren’s Novel Sets Release Date At Netflix View All August 28, 2026 11:26am Jacob Elordi as Hig in 20th Century Studios' THE DOG STARS. Fabio Lovino/20th Century Studios SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Dog Stars now out in theaters. Ridley Scott ’s newest film, The Dog Stars , is based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel of the same name. Mark L. Smith’s screenplay made several noticeable changes to the story, some of which provide more action in the plot and propel the film forward. The Dog Stars centers Jacob Elordi ’s mechanic-turned-pilot Hig, who is one of the lone survivors of a flu pandemic and follow-up blood disease, as he navigates post-apocalyptic Colorado and neighboring states. Related Stories Red Carpet Premieres ‘The Dog Stars’ World Premiere Red Carpet: Jacob Elordi, Margaret Qualley, Rak The Dog & More Reviews ‘The Dog Stars’ Review: Jacob Elordi Searches For Last Gasp Of Humanity In Ridley Scott’s Sharp Postapocalyptic Thriller He only has ex-military misanthrope, Bruce Bangley ( Josh Brolin ) and his German shepherd dog Jasper to keep him company, and when Hig needs space from Bangley, he flies out in his yellow Cessna plane to visit Mennonite families, whose leader is played by Benedict Wong, and provide them with medical supplies from a hospital in Denver. Hig risks contagion by the children and their parents to help them out. Watch on Deadline For differences — big and small — in the book, which generated a surge in the library app Libby demand by 268.5% the week of release, versus The Dog Stars film, read on. The Plane The 1956 Cessna 182 is described as cream and blue in the book. Hig nicknames her The Beast, which seems more of an inner monologue moniker. He uses it to fly the perimeter of his and Bangley’s little haven where they’ve survived trespassers and other threats mostly because Bangley picks them off with his long-range rifle. In the film, the plane is yellow. Jasper’s Death L-R: Jasper and Jacob Elordi as Hig in 20th Century Studios’ THE DOG STARS Fabio Lovino/ 20th Century Studios In Heller’s book, Jasper passes somewhat peacefully in his sleep when Hig takes him up to the mountains to camp and fish. The dog had gone mostly deaf, and he was getting old, so Hig’s decision to camp out under some frost ended up being too much for the canine. In the film, Jasper dies after Bangley waits until the last minute to pick off some invaders that target Hig and his dog. Bangley does this because Hig wasn’t thorough with his air surveillance and missed the people that came at him and Bangley. One of their errant gunshots found the canine’s heart. In both the book and the film, this is what ultimately galvanizes Hig to go fly beyond their shelter and search for more. He had received a signal from Grand Junction airport years ago, so he wanted to see if anything could be found behind that transmission. How Hig Meets Cima & Pops When Hig touches down in the book near Cima’s ( Margaret Qualley ) and Pops’ (Guy Pearce) farm, tucked away like his shelter with Bangley, he meets an aggressive Pops right away who shoots at him a couple of times. Hig doesn’t help by provoking him with scrawled messages on paper, but eventually they get past it and he stays with them. In the film, Sarah the donkey leads Hig to their ranch of sorts, and he sees Cima first, but Pops is behind him in the shadows with a rifle and quickly descends on Hig, telling him to unload his weapons and stand slowly. Pops does not want Hig anywhere on their property, but Cima engages in some conversation with the pilot. (L-R) Jacob Elordi as Hig and Margaret Qualley as Cima in 20th Century Studios’ THE DOG STARS Fabio Lovino/20th Century Studios How Cima & Pops Leave With Hig In the book, Pops and Hig slowly come to the conclusion that they can leave the farm all together in the plane. After working through the equations to balance cargo, fuel and the plane’s weight, it’s concluded that Pops will drive out onto the highway and then join his daughter and Hig in the Cessna after they’ve taken off to burn some of the fuel. The film sees them hastily get in the plane when a large group of hostile people find their farm and attack them. Both Pops and Cima get in the plane after they’ve helped Hig clear a path for takeoff by chopping down trees and throwing rocks out of the way. The Reapers In Heller’s novel, the looming new threat were referred to as “The A-rabs” who had somehow gotten to the country and were causing trouble. The film describes them as Reapers. Hig captured their graffiti in the beginning of the film, and a hoard of them — covered in facepaint — attack both Cima and Pops’ camp as well as Bangley, who is left alone when Hig goes out to find Cima and Pops. In the book, readers don’t get to fully see the attack on Bangley because it’s told from Hig’s perspective and he’s gone, but the film expands to show the scene, parts in night vision radar. Bangley’s relieving survival is part of both the book and film. Grand Junction Cima, Pops and Hig explore Grand Junction both in the book and in the movie, but what goes down there is wildly different in the movie. They both involve prompting by a transmission from an older woman’s voice. In the book, when Hig tries to land there, a trip wire almost snags the Cessna and pulls them down to their deaths in a crash. They then land still and discover an old couple, who they kill, living in the radio tower with way too many cats. The film took this part up a notch with a surprise appearance from Allison Janney as Darlene, voice heard on the radio and leader of a strange cult-like group who have been living at the airport for a while. Darlene used to be a flight attendant, and she still dresses the part. She only deems Cima fit to “keep” in their strange compound because she has doctorial skills.

title: Rafael Manuel on Why the Golf Course in ‘Filipiñana’ Is a Metaphor for Inequality in the Philippines
full_text: Aug 28, 2026 11:15am PT Rafael Manuel on Why the Golf Course in ‘Filipiñana’ Is a Metaphor for Inequality in the Philippines By Jazz Tangcay Plus Icon Jazz Tangcay Artisans Editor @jazzt Latest Rafael Manuel on Why the Golf Course in ‘Filipiñana’ Is a Metaphor for Inequality in the Philippines 2 hours ago Dolly Parton’s Musical Will Still Open on Broadway ‘As Was Dolly’s Wish’ 3 days ago Dolly Parton Honored by Kacey Musgraves, Keith Urban, Reba McEntire: ‘We Will Always Love Her’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Divergent PR Rafael Manuel ’s new indie feature “ Filipiñana ,” which opens Friday in New York, is set against a backdrop of oppressive heat and drought. The narrative follows Isabel, a 17-year-old from the provinces of the Philippines, who gets a job at a prestigious golf resort. Manuel felt the golf course was the perfect setting for the film to explore societal inequities in the country. With the very first courses established on American military bases, the local elite eventually took over, making the golf course a center of power. Related Stories Instagram Head of Product Design Explains Thinking Behind That New Logo and Responds to Critics: 'It's Important for Us to Embrace the Future' Instagram Unveils 'More Modern' New Logo, and People Are Already Making Fun of It In his framing, the country club members are presented high in the frame to show the hierarchy structure, and the servants are presented low in the frame — an early shot shows Isabel sitting on the grass as she places a ball on the tee for a club member. Popular on Variety Manuel says, “That’s what attracted me to the golf course.” He adds, “When you think about it, it’s a good metaphor for the country in that it’s very large and situated on a very fertile plot of land that’s toiled on and worked on by so many people, but ultimately enjoyed and profited from by only a select few.” That, Manuel says, illustrates the class divide that has been so ingrained in the Philippines. Manuel spoke with Variety about how the film relates to the colonial past of the country, and the metaphorical symbolism of the golf course. He also talks about reflecting that through Isabel’s gaze and why she represents an awakening. Can you talk about your main characters Isable and Clara and what they represent and what you wanted their gaze to say? I very much get the notion that Clara is an outsider in all of this. The first image you see of Isabel is of her opening her eyes, and the last image you see of Clara is of her closing her eyes. For me, that’s very much representative of their narrative arcs. Isabel’s journey is one of awakening and remembering the past, seeing it and hearing it. Whereas Clara’s journey is one into slumber, inaction, passivity, and perpetuating the system. Clara is a tragic character. Isabel, on the other hand, is a heroic character because I feel like Isabel moves towards action, and Clara moves towards inaction.” What went into that casting process and finding Jorrybell Agoto as Isabel and Carmen Castellanos as Clara? Clara is a non-actor, but Isabel was in the short. It was only her second time acting, and she was a very inexperienced actor. My directing style is to try to get out of the way as much as possible, so I spent a lot of time building the world of the character and of the film. When it comes to being on set, I try to direct them as little as possible because I trust all the work that we both did in pre-production. Freedom is such an important part of acting because every single decision and gesture that they make, they have to freely choose it. That’s how you get good acting. What I really look for in actors is playfulness because I see playfulness as a sort of resistance. What we try to do is build all these restrictions around them and then see how their playfulness and their autonomy express themselves through the parameters we’ve set. Can you talk about working with your production designer Tatjana Honegge and cinematographer Xenia Patricia in terms of establishing the film’s visual language. What did you want to say? It was very much a team effort. I’d also like to mention Vincent Villa. He’s a French sound designer based in Cambodia, and I feel like sound has a very important role to play in this film — even in the visual aesthetic — because sound guides the eye on where to look. I feel like the conversations we had were about developing an oral grammar that could give shape, texture, color, and sound to this invisible violence that we were very interested in exploring. A lot of the conversations I had with Xenia were about my obsession with landscape photography and how it’s been used in different contexts as a colonial tool. Susan Sontag’s “On Photography” talks about how the American West was colonized through landscape photography. If you go through the Philippine archive of the turn of the 20th century — around the 1800s and 1900s — you’ll see that the Philippines was also colonized through photography. Simon Schama writes about this in his book “Landscape and Power.” He talks about how landscape is a projection of man’s imagination onto rock, grass, and water. So the question naturally arises: Whose imagination is being projected? These colonial themes — this dreamwork of imperialism — very much inform the visual language of “Filipiñana.” You’re constantly seeing characters framed in these wide landscapes, and their small actions become a form of resistance to the colonizing gaze. A lot of the film is slow in terms of pacing, allowing moments to breathe. What was behind this choice? The slowness, for me, has a twofold purpose. First, it really helps communicate the heat and lethargy — the kind of lethargy that the Filipino humidity and the stifling 50-degree heat of a Filipino summer can induce. When you think about why the Philippines has stayed the same for so long — why the country has struggled with the same problems for so long — I think the heat has a part to play in that. If you’ve ever been in heat like that, so humid and sticky, you realize quite quickly that it’s like a quagmire. It makes action so hard to do because all you want to do is lie down. The slow pacing of the film was meant to communicate that. The second reason behind the deliberate pacing of the film was that I really wanted to capture this Filipino experience of waiting for change. What do you want people to take away from watching this? I feel like so much of what we’re trying to do is create a space for the viewer to exercise their autonomy—autonomy of sight, hearing and feeling. I say that because the way the drama is structured is very minimal. I feel like conventional narrative, in a way, is a form of gentrification. When you take into consideration how so many spaces — not just in the Philippines but around the world — are privatized, you realize you can step out of your house and, in five seconds, you’re being sold something by a billboard. Actually, you don’t even need to step out of your house; you can just go on Instagram. So, we really tried not to be didactic and instead create an autonomous space for viewers to practice their autonomy — or to be autonomous, if they choose to be. So when you ask me what I want them to take away, it’s hard to say because they can take away whatever it is they want to take away. The film’s designed like that. I guess for me, one of the main things I’m interested in hearing from audiences after a screening is: How did they view the ending? Did they view it as an optimistic ending, or did they view it as a pessimistic one? This interview has been edited and condensed. title: ‘Hooters: The Movie’ In The Works About Chicken-Wing Eatery’s Origins
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Starburns Industries’ Tom Hanks Pic ‘Lincoln In The Bardo’ Adds Willem Dafoe, Jonathan Bailey & Peter Dinklage Melissa Hirschenson Exits Innovative, Launches The Hirschenson Group ‘Hooters: The Movie’ In The Works About Chicken-Wing Eatery’s Origins View All August 28, 2026 11:08am Original Hooters Archives EXCLUSIVE: It’s about to get spicy on the big screen — there’s a movie about famous chicken-wing chain Hooters in the works. Hooters: The Movie is being independently produced by the chain’s original founding partners and is being directed by Emmy-nominated filmmaker Jon Rosenbaum ( Woody Woodpecker Goes to Camp, Benchwarmers 2: Breaking Balls ) off a screenplay by Ed Droste, Phil Olson and Chuck Melcher. Casting is underway, led by casting directors Lisa London and Catherine Stroud of London/Stroud Casting. Based on the real events behind Hooters’ founding, Hooters: The Movie centers on Ted and Lenny, two lifelong friends from a small town in Iowa who accidentally launch a national restaurant empire, only to find everything they built threatened by the federal government. The adventure begins when Ted becomes infatuated with Diane, whom he first sees from afar when featured in a spring break commercial. Determined to find her in real life, Ted talks a hesitant Lenny into joining him on a road trip to Clearwater Beach, FL. Diane would later become the very first Hooters Girl. title: Owen Thiele on Portraying Queer Friendship in ‘Adults,’ Working With Connor Storrie and Being a ‘Nepo Grandchild’
full_text: Aug 28, 2026 11:01am PT Owen Thiele on Portraying Queer Friendship in ‘Adults,’ Working With Connor Storrie and Being a ‘Nepo Grandchild’ By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Meg Stalter on ‘Oh, Mary’, Advice for Bowen Yang and Preparing Her Emmys Red Carpet Look With Paul Downs: ‘It’s in the Works’ 5 hours ago Jemima Kirke on Her Marc Jacobs Campaign, Fashion Week Chaos and Why Jessa’s Style in ‘Girls’ ‘Doesn’t Appeal’ to Her 23 hours ago The Best Celebrity Fragrance Campaigns in 2026: Zendaya, Dakota Johnson, Alexander Skarsgård and More 1 day ago See All Getty Images for Meta Owen Thiele has a lot more riding on “ Adults ” this time around. The FX comedy returned for its second season Aug. 27 with an audience now invested in its messy, co-dependent group of twentysomethings. Thiele, who plays Anton, says the cast spent much of the wait for renewal worried the show might not come back at all. “But I feel like now we have a little, tiny, beautiful cult following that hopefully will stick by us and get us that third season..” Related Stories Instagram Head of Product Design Explains Thinking Behind That New Logo and Responds to Critics: 'It's Important for Us to Embrace the Future' Instagram Unveils 'More Modern' New Logo, and People Are Already Making Fun of It That was the mood when Thiele sat down with Variety at an Instagram-hosted dinner at Palma in New York celebrating the new season. It can be hard to wrangle even the closest friends to a weeknight event, especially only one day after a booze-heavy premiere the previous night. But Thiele is unquestionably popular. Bowen Yang, Molly Gordon and Mary Beth Barone were just a few of his bold-faced friends who made their way to the West Village for a multi-course Italian meal and many, many dirty martinis. Popular on Variety Instagram also used the dinner to spotlight Instants, its newer feature for sending spontaneous photos through DMs, while Thiele is set to share behind-the-scenes content from the event on the platform’s @notfit4main account. Getty Images for Meta Getty Images for Meta Getty Images for Meta One reason for Thiele’s bursting-at-the-seams friend group is his growing list of Imdb credits. The 29 year-old also appears in Prime Video’s “Overcompensating,” where his character George represents a very different kind of queer friendship than Anton does, and he’s headed to the big screen in “Peaked,” Molly Gordon’s upcoming comedy, alongside Connor Storrie and Dua Lipa. He’s also writing “Off Color,” a semi-autobiographical Amazon comedy inspired by his experience growing up Black and gay in a white Jewish family. The project pulls from his fascinating family history: Thiele is the son of music producer Bob Thiele Jr. and the grandson of iconic record producer Bob Thiele (“What a Wonderful World,” which Thiele co-wrote for Louis Armstrong, might ring a bell.) Susie Essman, known for her iconic role in “Curb Your Enthiusiasm,” is set to play Owen’s mother. Below, Thiele talks to Variety about portraying queer friendship on screen, being a “nepo grandchild” and working with Connor Storrie and Dua Lipa: What can we expect from Season 2 of “Adults” — and Anton and Paul? Well, a lot happened. A lot happened. So I’m invested too. When I got those scripts, I was immediately reading. I was hoping that the kiss was addressed and it is but it’s addressed in a way that I think people wouldn’t expect. Like avoidant-attachment vibes? Sort of, sort of. It’s sort of like me in a relationship. I feel like you pull from your own life a lot for the character. Yes, I do, I do, I do. A lot of people would say I can’t act because of that. But the writers did such a brilliant job crafting this season because it doesn’t feel at all expected, and there are so many twists and turns that when I was filming it, I was like, “What? This is happening?” I couldn’t believe it. You’re in “Overcompensating”, too: the two shows reflect very different types of queer friendships. What do you think might have been missing in representations of queer friendship before, and what do those two separate arcs bring to it? I think “Overcompensating” does such a brilliant job of showing someone who isn’t comfortable with themselves finding solace and space in people who are comfortable with themselves. And I think what “Adults” does is show this immediate comfortability and coziness. Sexuality isn’t even uttered. But I think they’re two very important stories to tell. One is what I felt in high school. I came out in high school, and I was very much looking for somebody who I could relate to in that way, which is Benny [Benito Skinner] to George [Thiele]. And I feel like in “Adults,” I’m kind of where I am now, where it’s just unspoken and unsaid and it doesn’t really matter. I have to ask about “Off Color.” I imagine the “nepo baby” conversation is going to come up. How are you feeling about putting something this personal out there? One hundred percent. Everyone thinks I’m a nepo baby. I don’t think my dad was successful enough for me to be a nepo baby. But your grandpa was successful. I was on his Wikipedia today! No, my grandpa — I am. No, no, he was successful. I am a nepo grandchild, for sure. I’m scared, and I’m also ready. I’m like, you know what? I want to put myself out there in every way possible and see what happens. Some things will not be received well, and I’m ready for that. And hopefully other things will be. What have the conversations with your family been like while writing? It’s hilarious. It feels like therapy. It’s family therapy. My mom will be like, “I never said that.” And I’m like, “You definitely said that.” We’re all working through things, and I’m working through things as I write this show. I’m not running things by them. I’m more like sending them scripts, and my mom being like, “Why’d you make me a bitch?” Susan Essman is playing her. How did she get involved? I met with her. I sat with her and explained my life story to her, and she, for some reason, wanted to be involved, which is so crazy to me still. She’s Jewish, my parents are Jewish. But more than that, she’s an idol. She’s one of my comedy idols. She’s a comedy legend. So I feel very lucky. I can only think of her as her character in “Curb Your Enthusiasm.” What kind of energy does she bring playing your mom? My mom is a helicopter mom, but Owen in the show is front seat in the helicopter. He is obsessed with her being that way. So it’s the back-and-forth. It’s the enabling. It’s the codependency. She’s not really a yeller. She’s definitely a crier. She cries at everything. It’s a lack of boundaries. I haven’t seen Susie play this, which I think will be fun. Going back to “Peaked,” what was it like working with Connor Storrie? Connor is a dream. He is not only a very attractive man, he is so beyond talented. I interviewed him for my podcast, and afterward I was like, “Oh God, you are a dream.” And then I got to work with him after that. He was just down to play. Everyone on “Peaked” was just down to fucking clown. We were all down to do whatever Molly [Gordon] wanted us to do. Molly has such a great, beautiful, clear vision. What was it like being directed by Molly, who you’re so close to? She’s my best friend. It felt like we were kids again. I’ve known her since I was two. I’ve been in plays with her. She has directed me before. When I auditioned for “SNL,” she was very involved and was kind of directing my [audition] sketches for “SNL.” She’s been directing me for years, so this just felt like a natural progression. What’s your overall vibe with posting on social media? Oh my God, I love Instagram. I posted on Instagram twice today. In-feed. I think people are sick of me. I think people are unfollowing. I’m also like, who the fuck cares? Post when you have a hot photo. You have a hot photo, you want people to see it — post that shit. Who cares? Let’s not be precious with our dumps. Let’s just post when we like something. I want to go back to 2016 Instagram, where you’re posting a photo of something you like. full_text: Aug 28, 2026 11:01am PT Music Industry Moves: Warner Music and Blavatnik Family Foundation Announce 2026 Grantees; Spotify Ups Joe Hadley By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Music Industry Moves: Warner Music and Blavatnik Family Foundation Announce 2026 Grantees; Spotify Ups Joe Hadley 2 hours ago Nile Rodgers & Chic to Headline DKMS Cancer Benefit Gala in New York 2 days ago Warner Chappell Music Promotes Gabz Landman to Executive VP of A&R 4 days ago See All The Warner Music Group / Blavatnik Family Foundation Social Justice Fund has announced its first slate of 2026 grantees – a docket that includes 17 organizations and an investment of almost $6 million. Since its launch in 2020, the $100 million fund has committed more than $52 million to organizations that focus on criminal justice reform, education, and arts and culture to help advance equity. This latest docket includes six new grantees, with a focus on organizations using music as a tool to drive social progress. First-time grantees include Atlanta Music Project ,which provides tuition-free music training, performance opportunities, and college and career preparation to students in under-resourced Atlanta neighborhoods; Brooklyn Youth Sports Club ’s VOICES (Vibrations Of Inner-City Excellence and Success), which helps Black and Latino youth express themselves through songwriting, performing, and sound engineering; Classical Pride , a music festival celebrating LGBTQAI+ composers and musicians across classical music; and Generator , the music development organization that ensures that artists, talent, and creative professionals across the North of England have the opportunities, connections, and support to build sustainable careers. Over the next five years, it will support the creation and maintenance of 75 new prison libraries in the United States through new grantee Freedom Reads . title: ‘Stuart Fails’ Stars Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus Reveal Filming Episode 6 Scene “Was Terrifying”
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails’ Stars Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus Reveal Filming Episode 6 Scene “Was Terrifying” Tracy Oliver & Issa Rae Open Marriage Drama Heats Up TV Marketplace – The Dish Ellen Pompeo To Star In ‘Not A Sound’ Drama In Works At Hulu From David E. Kelley Productions View All August 28, 2026 10:22am Story Arc (L-R): Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus in 'Stuart Fails To Save the Universe' HBO Max SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 6 of HBO Max ‘s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . In Episode 6 of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe, the quartet of accidental heroes Stuart Bloom ( Kevin Sussman ), Denise ( Lauren Lapkus ), Bert (Brian Posehn) and Barry Kripke (John Ross Bowie) find themselves in a universe where people have descended from cows; they eat plants and chew their cud. Kripke and Bert want to leave, Stuart and Denise opt to stay, leading to the former duo being stuck falling in an endless void in-between universes. After meeting a new version of Raj (Kunal Nayyar) — who does not mention the broken device his post-apocalyptic self almost fixed in the first episode — and getting scolded by Stuart from another dimension, Stuart and Denise somehow order a second copy of the machine and soon find themselves falling through the void alongside Kripke and Bert. Related Stories News Everything We Know About 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 So Far News 'Backrooms': A24's Highest Grossing Pic Ever Sets Fall Streaming Date On HBO Max Turns out the horror on their faces was not just acting but the screams were hard to muster, Sussman and Lapkus told Deadline. “There were so many things that were crazy, I think being in the Matrix was insane, we were all with our bald caps in goo pods, and then we were on high wires, like flying, being dropped 30 feet in the air to shoot the falling-through-the-void scene, that was very scary,” Lapkus said about their experience filming Season 1 of the Big Bang Theory spinoff. “The high wire one in particular, the scene was we’re being dropped, falling through the air, and we’re supposed to be screaming,” Sussman said. “And what Lauren and I discovered both simultaneously the first time we were dropped, it was so much faster and scarier than we thought that neither of us were able to scream.” Added Lapkus, “When you’re actually scared, you can’t scream. It’s kind of like those nightmares that I’ve had over and over again, where I’m trying to scream and I can’t. When you’re falling and you’re actually scared, you just swallow it, we’re choking. Yeah, it was terrifying.” (You can watch the video below.) Speaking of choking, there was a lot of that in the episode with all the food regurgitating. “Lots of hay, lots of grass, yeah, lots of choking,” Lapkus said. Dog Days Of August: ‘Coyote Vs. title: Ron Perlman, Shohreh Aghdashloo & Cuba Gooding Jr. Set For Golden Dunes Jury Duty In Dubai
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Ron Perlman, Shohreh Aghdashloo & Cuba Gooding Jr. Set For Golden Dunes Jury Duty In Dubai Venice: Palestine-Israel Conflict Set To Be Hot-Button Topic As Open Letter Calls For Festival To Take Concrete Action In Support Of Palestine ‘Fjord’ Trailer: Neon Unveils Cristian Mungiu’s Palme D’Or Winner With Renate Reinsve & Sebastian Stan View All August 28, 2026 10:15am Ron Perlman, Shohreh Aghdashloo & Cuba Gooding Jr. Getty Images EXCLUSIVE: Dubai ’s reputation as a travel and entertainment destination has taken a battering in recent months as the emirate got caught in the crosshairs of the U.S.-Iran war but this has not put a stop to the fledgeling Golden Dunes Festival. Ali and Zeus Zamani , the L.A.-based filmmaking duo behind AZ Filmz , are pushing on with a second edition of the event they spearheaded last year in partnership with Ben Coen, Scott Carlson and Don Worley. After an inaugural edition revolving around an awards ceremony, the second edition has been expanded to three days and will feature a program of screenings, panels and workshops. Related Stories Casting Ron Perlman Latest To Join Amazon MGM's Horror Film 'Seasons' From Drew Hancock Casting Charlie Hunnam Gets 'Sons Of Anarchy' Gang Back Together For FX Meta-Series 'Legends' The event announced on Friday that Hellboy star Ron Perlman , Oscar-nominated actress Shohreh Aghdashloo ( House of Sand and Fog ) and Jerry Maguire Oscar winner Cuba Gooding Jr. have signed on as the first wave of jurors for the second edition. Watch on Deadline Perlman and Aghdashloo will take particularly active roles, joining panels and workshops alongside fellow jurors and invited industry guests. “Movies don’t really recognize borders. A great story can come from Los Angeles, Tehran, Seoul or Dubai, and if it’s truthful, it reaches you. That’s what festivals can do at their best, bring filmmakers into the same room and let audiences discover voices they might never otherwise encounter,” said Perlman. Gooding Jr. added, “Cinema has always been one of the great bridges between cultures. Having participated in Golden Dunes in its first year, I saw firsthand the kind of international exchange that Dubai can create. It is a city where filmmakers and audiences from different parts of the world naturally come together, and there is real value in creating a space where voices from East and West can meet through storytelling.” The second edition will run from November 28 to 30, with the Golden Dunes Awards taking place on November 29th at the Belcanto at Dubai Opera rooftop venue in downtown Dubai. “Our first year was about establishing Golden Dunes. Year two is about opening it up. We want filmmakers coming to Dubai for three days, not simply attending an awards ceremony sitting in a room with people like Ron and Shohreh,” said Ali Zamani . “It’s about their experiences, discovering films from other countries and building relationships with filmmakers they might never otherwise meet.” The first wave of the jury panel combines several generations and areas of filmmaking. Perlman’s credits include Hellboy , Sons of Anarchy , Nightmare Alley and Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio . Aghdashloo received an Academy Award nomination for House of Sand and Fog and won an Emmy for House of Saddam , with subsequent credits including The Expanse and The Flight Attendant . Gooding Jr. won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for Jerry Maguire after breaking through in John Singleton’s Boyz n the Hood , with additional credits including A Few Good Men , Men of Honor and The People v. title: Spotify Names Joe Hadley VP of Global Music Content and Partnerships
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All August 28, 2026 10:15am Joe Hadley Courtesy of Spotify Spotify has promoted Joe Hadley to vice president of global music content and partnerships, the company announced on Friday. Hadley, who has been at Spotify since 2022, will now oversee both the streaming service’s music editorial and partnerships teams, and he’ll work directly with artists, labels and music publishers. Hadley will report to Charlie Hellman, Spotify’s SVP and Global Head of Music. Previously, Hadley’s title was global head of music partnerships and audience. “Editorial is a key part of bringing an essential human touch to Spotify,” Hellman said in a statement. “The team’s judgment and taste is what fans and artists rely on. Joe’s capable leadership will keep artist advocacy at the center of our work and bring even more impact to the programming we do.” Along with Hadley’s promotion, J.J. Italiano has also been named of Head of Editorial. He will report to Hadley. Prior to joining Spotify, Hadley was a prolific booking agent, serving as the head of hip-hop and R&B at CAA, where his clients included Beyoncé and A$AP Rocky. Before then, he was an agent at Windish. Italiano had his first stint at Spotify from 2017 to 2019 before heading to YouTube in 2020. He came back to Spotify in 2022. THR

title: SCAD Savannah Film Festival Returns for 29th Year
full_text: Aug 28, 2026 10:15am PT SCAD Savannah Film Festival Returns for 29th Year By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest SCAD Savannah Film Festival Returns for 29th Year 3 hours ago ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Gameplay Trailer Shows Weapons Destroying Planet in the Series’ Finale (Gaming News Roundup) 1 day ago Dolly Parton Has One Last Song Buried in a Time Capsule: ‘My Place In History’ 2 days ago See All Getty Images for SCAD SCAD Savannah Film Festival returns for its 29th year on Oct. 24 through Oct. 31. The eight-day university-led festival in Georgia will host exclusive screenings, competition films, feature films, documentaries, shorts, animated films, panel discussions and workshops. Visiting industry professionals and students of SCAD School of Film and Acting and School of Animation and Motion Media can get to know each other through master classes, coffee talks, portfolio reviews and more. Related Stories Instagram Head of Product Design Explains Thinking Behind That New Logo and Responds to Critics: 'It's Important for Us to Embrace the Future' Instagram Unveils 'More Modern' New Logo, and People Are Already Making Fun of It Variety returns with its “Artisans to Watch” hosted by Jazz Tangcay and “Pixels and Pencils” hosted by Clayton Davis. Popular on Variety Returning programs also include The “Docs to Watch” series, hosted by Scott Feinberg of The Hollywood Reporter, spotlighting the 10 best documentaries of the year. Entertainment Weekly will host its “Breaking Big” panel recognizing the next generation of Hollywood talent. Deadline is also set to return with its “TV Sidebar” highlighting new series on television. Last year, Davis’ panel hosted the directors of “KPop Demon Hunters,” “Elio” and “TMNT,” as well as the helmer of “In Your Dreams,” “Arco” and “Little Amélie.” Chris Appelhans and Maggie Kang spoke about the global phenomenon that is “KPop Demon Hunters” and discussed the collaborative process behind the film while celebrating the freedom to present Korean culture in a bold, fresh way. “Let’s make these characters real — ugly at times, silly, and real hot,” Kang said with a laugh. Tangcay’s 10 artisans to watch panel featured “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen, “Sinners” cinematographer Autumn Durald Arkapaw and “Golden” singer and songwriter EJAE, all of whom went on to win Oscars. Durald Arkapaw made Oscar history by becoming the first woman to win in the best cinematography category. Speaking about working with director Ryan Coogler — the pair are reuniting for “The X-Files” reboot — she said, “We support each other. I’ve learned how to read the story through [Ryan’s] eyes, to understand what he needs to tell it and what is important to him.” As the first woman to shoot on 65mm, Durald Arkapaw said she was also grateful for the opportunity to continue opening doors for more representation in cinematography and to be an inspiration for female cinematographers. “It means the world when young girls, or film students of similar heritage, come up to me and express their gratitude, not just for the work, but for the fact that they can see someone like themselves behind the camera.” SCAD Savannah Film Festival is one of the largest in the Southeast U.S. with more than 74,000 people in attendance. Last year, SCAD screened 26 Oscar-nominated films, including eight of the Best Picture nominees. Stars who attended in 2025 included Best Actress Rose Byrne (“If I Had Legs I’d Kick You”), Best Supporting Actress Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas (“Sentimental Value”) and Best Casting winner Cassandra Kulukundis (“One Battle After Another”). Over 200 SCAD alumni also worked on 21 of the films nominated for Oscars including seven of the 10 Best Picture Nominees, three nominees for Best Animated Feature, and every nominee for Best Visual Effects. Festival passes for 2026 are available now. Individual event tickets will go on sale Oct. 2 online at filmfest.scad.edu or in person at the SCAD Box Office at 216 E. Broughton St. in Savannah. title: How ‘Idiots’ Director Macon Blair Conjures Big Laughs From the Year’s Cruelest Villain: ‘He’s Actually a Monster That Has to Be Captured Before More People Get Hurt’
full_text: Aug 28, 2026 10:15am PT How ‘Idiots’ Director Macon Blair Conjures Big Laughs From the Year’s Cruelest Villain: ‘He’s Actually a Monster That Has to Be Captured Before More People Get Hurt’ By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Tom Hardy Gets X-Rated About Kathy Bates, Raps About Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin and Recites Shakespeare on His Wild New Album 3 hours ago How ‘Idiots’ Director Macon Blair Conjures Big Laughs From the Year’s Cruelest Villain: ‘He’s Actually a Monster That Has to Be Captured Before More People Get Hurt’ 3 hours ago FilmQuest Announces 2026 Lineup: Jamie Lee Curtis, Britt Lower and Rhea Seehorn Among Stars of Genre Films at Utah Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Steve Swisher; Courtesy of IFC Entertainment “This guy really does need to be contained, because he’s got such potential for danger and violence and mayhem.” Macon Blair is describing the antagonist of his latest movie. He’s no stranger to menacing genre fare, as evidenced by the two other films he wrote and directed: 2017’s “I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore” and 2023’s “Toxic Avenger” reimagining. But despite pitch-black elements, “ Idiots ,” in theaters Friday via Independent Film Company, is a rollicking comedy. In it, two knuckleheads — the well-intentioned and religious Davis (O’Shea Jackson Jr.) and sleazy bro Mark (Dave Franco) — get a job chauffeuring troubled teens to rehab. While their first ward, Sheridan Kimberley (Mason Thames), appears to be just another troubled rich kid, he turns out to be way too dangerous for his clueless caretakers. Related Stories Instagram Head of Product Design Explains Thinking Behind That New Logo and Responds to Critics: 'It's Important for Us to Embrace the Future' Instagram Unveils 'More Modern' New Logo, and People Are Already Making Fun of It Having Sheridan actually be a cruel person was one of the key audience expectations the writer-director hoped to flip in the pursuit of laughs. Popular on Variety “It was about wanting to have the most formidable villain possible for these guys to go up against, and just play off the idea that audiences are smart and they’ve seen a lot of movies,” Blair says. “If you see a premise like this … ‘There’s two dumbbells that have a kid in the car.’ Your expectations are probably going to be that at some point along the way they will give him some advice or wisdom or a hug and he will be redeemed. He’ll get straightened out sooner or later. I really like the idea of taking the wheel in the complete opposite direction, where at a certain point you realize, ‘No, he’s actually a monster that has to be captured before more people get hurt,’ and playing off people’s expectations.” Sheridan’s cruelty also fueled the film’s oft-shifting tone, which keeps audiences uncomfortably guessing what cringy situation comes next. Without giving away too much, the film’s grossest scatological joke happens right before Sheridan has a sinister scene with a sex worker (Kiernan Shipka). “There’s this big, extremely over-the-top gross-out comedy punchline, and then about 10 seconds later, it goes 100 degrees in the opposite direction,” Blair says. “It’s meant to be whiplash that resets the tone of the movie. As soon as that happens, we’re back into the jokes, but in theory, that clenched feeling from that one moment remains, and that’s how you feel about Sheridan for the rest of the movie. When they’re running around the block trying to capture him, it’s not as cartoonish as it otherwise would be.” “Idiots” takes the structure of a road trip movie, as Davis and Mark work desperately to keep Sheridan under control and bring him to rehab. But along the way they reckon with Mark’s busted car, a werewolf-obsessed rapper (Nicholas Braun, in an outrageous role), a militant kidnapper (Peter Dinklage), bad drug trips and more. Beyond the plot, Blair and his DP Guillermo Garza hoped to give the comedy a dynamic visual style. Despite the tight indie schedule, Blair says all of this pressure helped make the movie stronger due to creative problem solving. “Because the schedule was so short, there were a lot of times where we had a very detailed shot listed/storyboarded plan going in. But we would get in the day, and there wasn’t going to be enough time to get all of it,” Blair says. “So a lot of times on the fly, Guillermo and I would redistill the scene and say, ‘OK, if we thought we were going to do this moment in three shots, what’s the version of it where it’s one shot and we just do it with a move?’ It was one of those things where the limitations of time or light or whatever forced us to … I don’t mean ‘not be precious about it.’ It’s kind of the opposite of that. To really drill down on: ‘gun to my head, what can we afford to lose?’ So the scenes become as specific as possible, because it’s really just the bare bones of what you very essentially need. I’m not saying, ‘I would go into another movie asking for fewer days.’ I wouldn’t. But I loved how that happened, because if we had the luxury of ‘you can shoot as much as you want,’ I don’t think we would have come up with the same solutions, and it would have felt different. It would have felt a little less sharp.” The one comedic element Blair didn’t want to stick his neck out for? The much-discussed original title. The film premiered at this year’s Sundance Film Festival as “The Shitheads,” but was renamed “Idiots” once Independent Film Company acquired and dated the film. It wasn’t a war Blair felt like waging. “That was part of the conversation we had internally about changing the title: It wasn’t so much a full ‘You’re not allowed to do this.’ It was just a list of limitations,” he says. “It was a lot of things that had to do with where posters could be displayed in public, and how you could obscure the names. It started to feel like it was going to be an uphill battle promotion-wise with this movie. Given that it’s a smaller movie and it’s coming out in the summertime, and there are a ton of movies to compete with, we didn’t want to hamstring ourselves with, yes, it’s a funny title, but to cross your arms and say, ‘By God, I’ll have fewer people see the movie to hold on to this title.’ It seemed like cutting off your nose to spite your face. So we said, ‘Let’s just pivot to something that’s not going to give us that hassle.’” Watch the trailer for “Idiots” below.
